entries.title: Galápagos Islands
entries.answer: The Galápagos Islands lie far west of Ecuador’s mainland in the Pacific. Eruptions built the islands from the seafloor, so they were separated from the continent from the start. Plants and animals arrived over water in different ways, and their descendants changed over many generations. Some became different from living things elsewhere. Charles Darwin’s visit helped him think about how animals on separate islands can develop different shapes and habits.
facts: Giant tortoises and land iguanas live on the islands.
Ocean currents from different directions meet around the Galápagos.

entries.title: Grand Canyon
entries.answer: The Grand Canyon is a huge cut through rock in northern Arizona. Far below its rim, the Colorado River has been lifting and carrying away pieces of rock for millions of years. Rain and rockslides help widen the sides as the river keeps cutting. The canyon walls show stripes of different rocks. Some rock near the bottom is much older than the canyon itself, because it was already there when the river began cutting down.
facts: Parts of the canyon are over a mile deep.
Some rocks seen near the bottom formed more than a billion years ago.

entries.title: Great Barrier Reef
entries.answer: The Great Barrier Reef lies off Australia’s northeastern coast. It is made of thousands of separate reefs rather than one long unbroken wall. Small coral animals build hard skeletons, and over time new generations grow onto the old structures. The reefs leave hiding places and feeding spots for many animals. On a map some parts of the system meet open ocean, while others protect shallower stretches of sea closer to the shore.
facts: The Great Barrier Reef runs for about 2,300 kilometers along the northeastern side of Australia.

entries.title: How did a volcano help form Crater Lake?
entries.answer: Crater Lake in Oregon fills a deep bowl where a great volcano once stood. After an enormous eruption, the inside of Mount Mazama could no longer hold up the rock above it. Part of the mountain collapsed, making a basin called a caldera. Rain and melting snow later collected in the basin. There is no large river flowing in, and the lake can look deep blue when the sky is clear.
facts: Wizard Island formed from volcanic activity after the large collapse.

entries.title: How did Mammoth Cave get so many tunnels?
entries.answer: In Mammoth Cave in Kentucky, layers of limestone contain a maze of passages. Rain picks up gases from the air and soil, making water that can slowly dissolve limestone. It slips through tiny cracks and makes some of them larger. Changes in where water can flow over time can leave tunnels on different levels. Many passages above the present underground streams are dry enough for people to walk through.
facts: Limestone and moving water helped make the cave. Its name describes its huge size.

entries.title: How did people make rooms in Cappadocia’s rocks?
entries.answer: In Cappadocia in Türkiye, tall rock shapes rise from valleys and hills. Wind and water helped wear away layers of material from old volcanic eruptions, leaving some high pillars. In places the rock was soft enough for people to dig into, so they carved rooms, churches, and even routes below ground. This saved them from having to carry in all the stones for walls. Some rooms still hold paintings.
facts: Many tall pillars in Cappadocia are nicknamed fairy chimneys because of their shape.

entries.title: How did water build natural dams at Plitvice Lakes?
entries.answer: At Plitvice Lakes in Croatia, water runs from lake to lake over a series of waterfalls. It picks up dissolved minerals when it flows over and through some kinds of rock. Farther along, it can leave those minerals behind. Over many years, deposits of a rock called travertine grew into barriers that hold back water. Each barrier acts rather like a dam, making some water spill over it into the next lake.
facts: The barriers can keep changing as streams deposit minerals and wear away rock.

entries.title: Lake Baikal
entries.answer: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake in the world. Looking at the thin shape it makes on a map gives little hint of how much water is below the surface. The deep opening formed as large areas of rock moved apart. Baikal has fresh water and is home to some animals that live nowhere else, including a seal that spends its life far from any ocean.
facts: At its deepest, Lake Baikal is roughly a mile deep.
Lake Baikal contains a huge share of the fresh water found in the world’s lakes.

entries.title: Mount Kilimanjaro
entries.answer: Mount Kilimanjaro rises from the plains of northern Tanzania to the highest point in Africa. It is made of several volcanoes joined together. A climber passes through different environments, from wooded mountain slopes into cold, mostly bare country near the top. That change happens in a surprisingly short distance because the trail climbs so high. Near the equator the lowlands can be warm while the summit is cold enough for ice.
facts: Kilimanjaro’s highest point is nearly 5,900 meters above sea level.

entries.title: Victoria Falls
entries.answer: The Zambezi River spreads wide at the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe, then suddenly pours into a deep, narrow crack in the rock. The water hits with enough force to throw fine drops high above the cliffs. Wind blows this mist onto nearby land, watering plants even when rain has not fallen there. The volume of water changes with the season, so the falls do not always look exactly the same.
facts: Mosi-oa-Tunya is one of the local names for the falls, often translated as “the smoke that thunders.”

entries.title: What happens in the Singapore Botanic Gardens?
entries.answer: In Singapore’s Botanic Gardens, visitors walk among plants while workers grow, label, study, and care for them. A botanic garden keeps living plants together so researchers and visitors can compare how they grow. In Singapore’s tropical weather, the garden grows many kinds of orchids. It has also been a place to study useful plants. Looking after a living collection takes regular work as plants grow, move, or need new space.
facts: Some plants at the gardens are grown for study and others help visitors see the variety of plant life.

entries.title: What makes a place a World Heritage Site?
entries.answer: Some places hold clues about Earth or human history that people across the world can learn from. Countries can propose special places for an international list kept through UNESCO. A place on that list may be a building, a city, a natural area, or a mix. Protecting it can mean keeping an old structure safe, looking after land and water, or planning how people can visit without damaging the place.
facts: A named World Heritage Site can be important both for its natural features and for its role in people’s lives.

entries.title: What makes Old Faithful famous?
entries.answer: Old Faithful is a geyser in Yellowstone National Park. Water under the ground gets very hot, and steam and water rush out when enough pressure builds. The time between bursts changes, but people can often predict the next one from what happened in the last burst. That useful pattern is what makes it worth waiting to see. The geyser does not need a pump or anyone to turn it on.
facts: Old Faithful is one of many geysers in Yellowstone National Park.

entries.title: What shaped Yosemite Valley?
entries.answer: Yosemite Valley in California has huge granite cliffs, including El Capitan. Granite is a hard rock that formed when melted rock cooled deep underground. Later, glaciers moved through the valley. The heavy ice scraped rock and carried pieces away, helping make the valley wide and steep sided. As the ice melted, it left a valley with tall walls and streams that spill over the cliffs as waterfalls.
facts: You can see the valley’s wide U shape from above in some parts of Yosemite.

entries.title: What shapes make the Sydney Opera House easy to recognize?
entries.answer: The Sydney Opera House stands beside the harbor in Sydney, Australia. Its light-colored roofs look like pieces of shells, and some people think they look like sails. Under the roofs are halls where people can hear music and watch shows. To make the roof design possible to build, the shapes were worked out as pieces of a sphere, like sections cut from the surface of a big ball.
facts: The building is on a point of land that reaches into Sydney Harbour.

entries.title: Who carved the big stone figures on Rapa Nui?
entries.answer: Rapa Nui is a Chilean island far out in the Pacific Ocean. Its Indigenous Rapa Nui people carved large stone figures known as moai. Some figures stand on raised platforms, and others remain near the place where people cut them from volcanic rock. The figures show that the island’s stoneworkers created and moved very large objects with tools and methods that people still study. The Rapa Nui people and culture continue today.
facts: The figures generally show much more than a head, even when the rest is hard to see above ground.

entries.title: Why are some Mesa Verde homes tucked under cliffs?
entries.answer: At Mesa Verde in what is now Colorado, Ancestral Pueblo people built homes in openings under overhanging cliffs. A natural rock roof covered some of the living space, so builders could put up stone walls underneath it. Large sites held many rooms and open areas where people could gather. The cliff homes were one part of a bigger landscape where communities farmed and built other kinds of homes, including ones on flatter ground above.
facts: Cliff Palace is a well-known group of rooms built into one large sheltered opening.

entries.title: Why are some Venice streets made of water?
entries.answer: Venice in northeastern Italy grew across many low islands in a lagoon, a partly sheltered area of water near the sea. Waterways between the islands serve as long routes for boats. Bridges let people walk between many of the islands, and footpaths run beside some canals. A boat can reach docks and doorways beside the water, while people on foot follow a different set of routes through the same city.
facts: The Grand Canal is one of the main waterways through Venice.

entries.title: Why are the dunes at White Sands so white?
entries.answer: White Sands in New Mexico has dunes made mostly from gypsum, a light-colored mineral. Water can dissolve gypsum in nearby mountains, carry it down, and leave crystals behind as the water dries. The crystals break into smaller grains. Wind moves piles of those grains, giving the dunes their rippling shapes. It is unusual to find so much gypsum as sand because water can dissolve it again.
facts: Wind can change the position of a dune and draw small ripples on top of it.

entries.title: Why are the Everglades called a river of grass?
entries.answer: In South Florida, fresh water can move slowly across flat land in a broad, shallow sheet. Sawgrass and other plants grow up through it, so parts of the wetland can look more like a prairie than a narrow river. The amount of water changes with the seasons. Farther south, fresh water mixes with salt water. Where water comes from and how long it stays help shape which plants and animals can live there.
facts: Wetland channels called sloughs usually stay flooded longer than slightly higher ground nearby.

entries.title: Why are there so many rock arches in Arches National Park?
entries.answer: In eastern Utah, Arches National Park has many openings through red sandstone. Sandstone is made of grains that have stuck together into rock. Here, cracks and softer parts of the rock give water routes to work through. As pieces loosen and wear away, some openings grow. A hard rim can stay above a hole for a long time, making a natural arch. Arches can also break as the rock keeps changing.
facts: The famous Delicate Arch is one of many natural stone openings in the park.

entries.title: Why are there stone walls around Old Québec?
entries.answer: The older part of Québec City in Canada stands beside the St. Lawrence River. Some buildings stand on higher ground and others are below them near the river. People built walls and gates around the upper part long ago to help defend the place. Much of that wall survives, so you can still see how the fort and town fit together. Gateways connect the old streets with the rest of the city.
facts: Much of the lower town grew near the water, where people could reach ships.

entries.title: Why do some churches at Lalibela sit below ground level?
entries.answer: In Lalibela in Ethiopia, builders cut churches from rock instead of stacking up separate stones. For some of them, they removed rock from around the walls, leaving the outside in place, then cut rooms inside. The roof of a deeply cut church can come close to the level of the ground around it. Paths, trenches, and tunnels connect different parts of the site. People still use these churches for worship.
facts: One church, Biete Ghiorgis, has a shape like a cross when seen from above.

entries.title: Why does Devils Tower look like a bundle of stone pillars?
entries.answer: Devils Tower rises above nearby land in Wyoming. When melted rock underground cooled long ago, it shrank and cracked. The cracks separated the hard rock into tall columns, many with several flat sides. Softer rock around it wore away over many years, leaving the columns standing above the ground. Scientists agree about much of that story, but are still studying exactly how the original melted rock reached its place.
facts: The rocks piled at the base include pieces that broke from the tower.

entries.title: Why does Mont-Saint-Michel sometimes look like an island?
entries.answer: Mont-Saint-Michel is a rocky rise in a bay in France, with a village and a large abbey on it. At low tide, the water can move far out over the bay, leaving wide stretches of sand and mud exposed. At high tide, water spreads across that flat area and can surround the rock. The land is always there, but the moving edge of the sea changes what you see.
facts: The abbey sits high above the houses on the rock.

entries.title: Why does the Giant’s Causeway look paved with stone tiles?
entries.answer: On the coast of Northern Ireland, thousands of rock columns meet the sea at the Giant’s Causeway. Long ago, lava flowed over the land, cooled, and shrank. Cracks spread through the cooling rock, leaving columns with flat sides. Many tops have six sides, so from above they can look like a floor built from large tiles. The columns are made of basalt, a dark volcanic rock.
facts: The Giants in the landmark’s name belong to stories told about the place, while the rock preserves a record of volcanic activity.

entries.title: Why does the Hoh River valley grow such tall trees?
entries.answer: Moist air from the Pacific rises against Washington’s Olympic Mountains. As the air rises and cools, it can drop a great deal of rain on the Hoh River valley. Parts of the valley can receive about twelve feet of rain and other moisture in a year. Mild winters and cool summers help keep the woods damp. Tall Sitka spruce and western hemlock trees rise above the river valley, while ferns and moss grow below. Moss can even hang from branches far above the forest floor.
facts: The Hoh Rain Forest is named for the river that runs through the valley.

entries.title: Why was Borobudur built in rising terraces?
entries.answer: Borobudur is a large Buddhist temple on the island of Java in Indonesia. It is built in a series of terraces, or wide steps with room to walk along them. Some walkways pass walls carved with scenes. Higher up, rounded terraces hold bell-shaped stone structures called stupas. People can follow the paths around a level before going up. The arrangement is part of how the temple shows ideas about a spiritual journey.
facts: Some of the higher stone structures have openings that let light in around a Buddha figure.
